name: Skin-only facelift
summary: Lifting and trimming just the skin of the face; the oldest, simplest facelift, with milder recovery and a shorter-lived result than deeper techniques.
lead: A skin-only facelift is a form of rhytidectomy in which the surgeon lifts and redrapes the facial skin and removes the excess, without separately tightening or repositioning the deeper tissue layers such as the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) or facial muscles . It is the older, simpler approach to facelifting and is contrasted in the surgical literature with SMAS, deep-plane and composite techniques .

name: Upper blepharoplasty
summary: Removing excess upper-lid skin, muscle and fat through a crease incision; established surgery for hooding, with mostly surgeon-reported evidence.
lead: Upper blepharoplasty is surgery on the upper eyelids that removes or repositions excess skin, orbicularis oculi muscle and sometimes fat . The incision is placed in the natural eyelid crease so that the scar is concealed . It is performed for functional reasons, such as excess skin (dermatochalasis) obstructing the upper visual field, and for cosmetic reasons, such as hooded or tired-looking lids .

name: Fat repositioning (tear trough)
summary: Moving under-eye fat into the tear trough instead of cutting it out; documented in surgeon case series, not randomised trials.
lead: Fat repositioning is a lower-eyelid surgical technique in which orbital fat that would otherwise bulge as an under-eye bag is mobilised and moved over the infraorbital rim to fill the hollow below it, known as the tear trough . It contrasts with traditional lower blepharoplasty, in which herniated fat is simply removed.

name: CO2 laser blepharoplasty
summary: Eyelid surgery with a CO2 laser instead of a scalpel; small studies report less bleeding and bruising but the same final look.
lead: CO2 laser blepharoplasty is eyelid surgery in which a carbon dioxide laser is used as the cutting and coagulating instrument in place of a cold steel scalpel and electrocautery . It may be combined with laser resurfacing of the surrounding skin to treat periocular wrinkles .

name: Double eyelid suture (non-incisional)
summary: Stitch-only creation of an upper eyelid crease; fast and incision-free, but the crease can fade and buried sutures can injure the eye.
lead: Non-incisional double eyelid surgery, also called the buried-suture or suture-ligation method, creates an upper eyelid crease by passing sutures through the lid to bind the skin to deeper tissue such as the levator aponeurosis, without removing skin through an incision . It is a variant of East Asian blepharoplasty, aimed at people who naturally lack a supratarsal crease .

name: Le Fort I osteotomy
summary: Cutting and repositioning the upper jaw to fix bite and midface proportion; major surgery with a large clinical literature.
lead: A Le Fort I osteotomy is an orthognathic (jaw) operation in which the upper jaw, or maxilla, is cut horizontally above the roots of the upper teeth, freed, moved to a new position, and fixed in place, commonly with titanium plates and screws . It is used to correct bite problems and skeletal jaw discrepancies such as vertical maxillary excess, to treat cleft-related maxillary deficiency, and as part of maxillomandibular advancement for obstructive sleep apnoea . It is also used for facial aesthetic goals, because moving the maxilla changes midface projection and proportion .
claims: Le Fort I can produce an unattractive 'chimp mouth' result in some patients.

name: T-osteotomy genioplasty (mini V-line)
summary: Korean chin-bone surgery that narrows and slightly lengthens the chin; supported by surgeon case reports, not trials.
lead: T-osteotomy genioplasty, commonly called the mini V-line operation, is a chin-bone procedure that narrows the chin and, in many descriptions, lengthens it. It originated in Korean craniofacial practice. The surgeon makes one horizontal and two vertical bone cuts, removes a trapezoid-shaped piece, and repositions and fixes the remaining chin segment with titanium plates.

name: Surgery-first orthognathic approach
summary: Jaw surgery done before (or without) braces; studied in cohorts, with treatment-time and stability findings that vary by study.
lead: The surgery-first orthognathic approach (SFOA) is a way of sequencing corrective jaw surgery in which the bone operation is done before, or without, the traditional period of pre-surgical orthodontic treatment with braces. Conventional orthognathic care uses braces before and after surgery, with the pre-surgical phase traditionally lasting up to about a year.

name: Custom PEEK jaw implant
summary: A patient-specific jaw implant in PEEK plastic; the material is established in spine and skull surgery, but no cosmetic jaw studies were found.
lead: A custom PEEK jaw implant is a patient-specific implant made of polyether ether ketone (PEEK), a semicrystalline thermoplastic, intended to augment or reconstruct the jaw. PEEK is used in spinal fusion devices and as a partial skull replacement in neurosurgery.

name: Maxillary distraction osteogenesis
summary: Gradual upper-jaw lengthening with a bone-stretching device, studied mainly in cleft and severe hypoplasia cases rather than cosmetic use.
lead: Maxillary distraction osteogenesis (MDO) is a surgical technique for advancing the upper jaw gradually. The bone is cut, a distraction device is attached, and the segments are slowly separated so new bone forms in the gap, rather than moving the jaw in one step as in conventional orthognathic surgery.

name: Mandibular distraction osteogenesis
summary: Gradual lower-jaw lengthening with a bone-stretching device, well documented in children with congenital conditions, unstudied for purely cosmetic use.
lead: Mandibular distraction osteogenesis (MDO) is a surgical technique that lengthens the lower jaw gradually. The bone is cut and the segments are slowly separated by a device, so new bone forms in the gap. The principle derives from Ilizarov's work on long bones, who showed bone forms when stretched along its axis at about 1 mm per day.

name: Total maxillary osteotomy
summary: Whole upper jaw cut and repositioned (Le Fort I) for long-face problems; a major, established jaw operation with solid surgical literature but little on looks outcomes.
lead: Total maxillary osteotomy, usually performed as a Le Fort I osteotomy, is an orthognathic (jaw) operation in which the whole upper jaw is cut free from the skull base and moved to a new position, then fixed in place. In the medical literature it is used for conditions such as vertical maxillary excess (often called long face syndrome), open bite and under-grown upper jaws, for example in cleft lip and palate . In looksmaxxing culture it is classed as a hardmaxxing procedure, meaning a bone-level surgical change to facial structure.

name: Medpor chin implant
summary: Hard porous polyethylene chin implant that tissue grows into; established chin option with little comparative trial data.
lead: A Medpor chin implant is a chin augmentation implant made of high-density porous polyethylene, a hard, porous and slightly flexible material. Tissue grows into its pores, which anchors it and supports blood supply, but also makes it harder to remove than non-porous alternatives . It is one of several alloplastic (synthetic) options alongside silicone and expanded PTFE .

name: ePTFE (Gore-Tex) facial implant
summary: Gore-Tex-type porous synthetic implant used for chin, lip, nasolabial and nasal augmentation; cosmetic studies are small and mostly older.
lead: Expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE), best known under the brand name Gore-Tex, is a flexible, porous synthetic material used in facial implants for the chin, lips, nasolabial folds and nose, as well as in many non-cosmetic medical devices. Expanded PTFE was produced in 1969 by Robert Gore, who rapidly stretched heated PTFE to create a microporous structure; because it is nearly inert in the body and allows tissue to grow into it, it is used in vascular grafts, sutures, heart patches and other implants .

name: Silicone chin implant
summary: Soft, removable synthetic implant for chin projection; common option, with published evidence mostly on complications.
lead: A silicone chin implant is a solid, shaped alloplastic implant placed in front of the chin bone to increase projection. A general reference describes silicone as among the most commonly used chin implant materials: soft and flexible, but not bonding to tissue, so the pocket must be made precisely, with risks of movement, buckling or bone resorption; it can be removed easily .

name: Mersiline mesh implant
summary: Polyester mesh named as a facial-augmentation material, but backed by essentially no cosmetic data.
lead: Mersiline mesh is named in a general reference on chin augmentation as one of several alternative implant materials, described there as a mesh scaffold, alongside acellular dermal matrix and braided suture material (Supramid) . The name appears to correspond to Mersilene, a Dacron (polyester) surgical mesh used for decades in hernia repair, prolapse surgery and eyelid-lifting (frontalis suspension) procedures .

name: Mustardé otoplasty
summary: Mattress-suture ear pinning that builds the antihelical fold; a long-established technique backed mostly by retrospective series.
lead: Mustardé otoplasty is a technique for correcting prominent ears in which permanent mattress sutures are placed to create or deepen the antihelical fold, setting back the helical rim without cutting the cartilage. It is based on J. C. Mustardé's 1963 paper on correcting prominent ears with simple mattress sutures . A general reference classes it among techniques that keep the ear cartilage intact, describing it as an open method in which the cartilage at the back of the ear is exposed, a strip of skin removed and mattress sutures placed .

name: Furnas suture technique
summary: Concha-to-mastoid stitches that pin back a deep ear bowl; an established surgical technique with case-series evidence and a known recurrence risk.
lead: The Furnas suture technique is an otoplasty (ear surgery) method that sets back a prominent ear by placing permanent or long-lasting sutures between the conchal cartilage (the bowl of the ear) and the mastoid periosteum behind the ear. It was described by David Furnas in 1968 and is often paired with the Mustardé technique, which forms the antihelical fold with mattress sutures.

name: Stenström technique
summary: Ear pinning by scoring the front of the antihelix cartilage so it folds; long used surgically, supported by case series.
lead: The Stenström technique (Stenström otoplasty) is an ear-pinning procedure in which the front surface of the antihelical cartilage is scored or rasped so that the cartilage bends backward and forms a fold. It was described by Sten Stenström in 1963.

name: Merck stitch otoplasty
summary: A closed ear-pinning method using stitches through tiny stab incisions; documented but with little published outcome data.
lead: The Merck stitch is a closed, minimally invasive otoplasty method in which sutures are placed through small stab incisions to reshape the ear without cutting the cartilage. Wikipedia dates its publication to 2013.

name: Incisionless Fritsch otoplasty
summary: Ear pinning with needle-placed stitches through the skin and no incision; documented, but outcome data are thin.
lead: Incisionless (percutaneous) otoplasty, associated with Fritsch, places sutures through the skin with needles to shape the antihelix and conchal bowl, without a skin incision. Wikipedia dates Fritsch's publications on the method from 1995 to 2009 and notes it may be combined with superficial scoring of the cartilage.

name: Converse–Wood-Smith otoplasty
summary: A cartilage-cutting ear-pinning method using parallel full-thickness incisions to build a fold; older, with little modern human data located.
lead: The Converse–Wood-Smith technique forms an antihelix by making full-thickness incisions through the ear cartilage and shaping it with tubing sutures. Wikipedia describes it as two parallel cartilage incisions with sutures that create a more natural fold; Converse described a cartilage-incision method in 1955.

name: Earlobe reduction/repair
summary: Minor plastic surgery to mend torn or split earlobes or reduce large ones; many technique papers, small case series.
lead: Earlobe repair and reduction are surgical procedures that reshape or mend the earlobe. Repair addresses torn or split lobes, often from heavy earrings, trauma or gauged piercings, while reduction addresses oversized or protruding lobes.

name: Ear cartilage molding (EarWell)
summary: A newborn-only splint system that reshapes soft infant ear cartilage; studies report high correction rates when started in the first weeks, and it is not an adult option.
lead: Ear molding, also called infant ear splinting or newborn ear correction, is a non-surgical treatment for congenital ear deformities in which a small device is attached to a baby's ear for several weeks to reshape the cartilage. Conditions treated include prominent or cup ears, lop (lidding) ears, Stahl's ear, helical rim abnormalities, cryptotia and constricted ears . The EarWell Infant Ear Correction System is a commercial product built around this method .

name: Corner lip lift
summary: Surgical skin excision at the corners of the mouth to raise downturned commissures; evidence is surgeon case experience, and visible scarring is a recognised risk.
lead: A corner lip lift (also called corner of the mouth lift, commissure lift or smile lift) is a surgical procedure that raises the corners of the mouth, typically by removing a small, lens-shaped piece of skin at or above the oral commissure . It is performed to alter the resting angle of the mouth in people whose corners turn downward, and is often combined with an upper lip lift .
claims: A corner lip lift makes the mouth wider and lips look fuller.
The procedure can be used to set new facial proportions before other surgery such as jaw or chin implants.
Surgeons advise against the corner lift to protect white lip length, but some patients choose it anyway.

name: Gore-Tex lip implant (SoftForm)
summary: A tubular expanded-PTFE implant placed in the lip for permanent volume; the sources reviewed describe it only briefly and report implant movement and extrusion as risks.
lead: Gore-Tex lip implants are strips or tubes of expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) used for lip augmentation. Wikipedia describes them as 1.6 mm or 4.8 mm in diameter and names Advanta, UltraSoft and SoftForm as commercial versions .

name: Alloderm lip augmentation
summary: Lip volume from processed donor skin (AlloDerm) placed in rolls in the lip; sources reviewed give only a short description and one 2000 journal paper title.
lead: AlloDerm lip augmentation uses processed donor (cadaver) dermis to add volume to the lips. Wikipedia says it is placed in small rolls in the mucosa to add size, or in the vermilion to sharpen the lip border .

name: Dermalogen / Autologen
summary: Collagen injectables made from skin (the patient's own for Autologen, donor for Dermalogen); sources describe them as dermal fillers with short-to-moderate persistence and no allergy testing needed.
lead: Autologen and Dermalogen are injectable dermal fillers consisting of human tissue collagen matrix. Autologen is derived from the patient's own skin, and Dermalogen from donor (allogeneic) tissue .

name: Mucomuscular flap lip augmentation
summary: Surgical lip enlargement by moving intraoral tissue into the lip; the only source reviewed describes flaps generally as adding little volume.
lead: Mucomuscular flap lip augmentation refers to surgical lip enlargement using tissue from inside the mouth. Wikipedia describes lip augmentation by flaps, in which small strips of skin from near the lips or inside the mouth are moved to the lips, and says this adds little volume and produces only slight protrusion .

name: Lip plumper (capsaicin)
summary: A chili-based lip gloss that irritates the lips into swelling for a short while; the volume is brief and the evidence thin.
lead: A capsaicin lip plumper is a topical cosmetic applied to the lips that uses an irritant, most often capsaicin from chili peppers, sometimes with menthol, cinnamon, peppermint or ginger, to produce a brief tingling or burning sensation and temporary swelling that makes the lips look fuller. It is marketed as a non-injectable alternative to lip filler.
